hypothesis: An end-to-end automated RCA pipeline (collection, detection, AI-assisted hypothesis generation, and automated/assisted remediation) built from the companion repository reduces (a) time-to-detection for LLM incidents, (b) mean time to recover (MTTR), and (c) the rate of incorrect root-cause attributions compared to a baseline of manual, dashboard-driven investigation using the same observability data.

baseline.description: Manual, dashboard-driven RCA process using standard observability tools without the specialized automated RCA components from the companion repository.
components: Standard metrics/logs/traces collection (e.g., OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, ELK) already integrated with the sample LLM application.
No dedicated RCA pipeline: incidents are investigated manually by an on-call engineer using dashboards, ad-hoc queries, and log searches.
No automated hypothesis generation, clustering, or RCA-specific correlation; any correlations are discovered manually.
Remediation decisions (rollbacks, routing updates, prompt fixes, tool disables) are performed manually via configuration changes or feature flags.
Incidents are simulated using the same replay workloads as the treatment, but automation-specific services are disabled.

process.triggering: A synthetic incident is initiated; only generic alerts (e.g., latency, error-rate, or business KPI alerts) fire.
process.investigation: A single experienced engineer uses pre-built dashboards and ad-hoc queries to identify scope, suspected component, and root cause. They capture steps and timestamps in a structured incident log template.
process.remediation: Engineer applies changes via documented runbooks (routing config change, prompt rollback, data pipeline fix, or tool disable) and confirms recovery via dashboards.
process.documentation: Engineer records final root cause, remediation, and timeline. This documentation is later used as ground truth for correctness and false-diagnosis evaluation.

treatment.description: End-to-end automated RCA system built from the companion repository, instrumented into the same sample LLM stack and used to handle the same incident replays.
components: RCA signal ingestion layer wired to the application’s metrics/logs/traces and structured LLM interaction events (from earlier chapters).
Detection and localization service for LLM-specific failures (hallucination spikes, latency/cost regressions, tool failures) with dedicated alerts.
AI-assisted hypothesis generation and ranking pipeline that fuses signals from infrastructure, LLM content evaluation, routing decisions, and data/tooling pipelines.
Incident correlation and clustering to group related anomalous events into coherent incident contexts.
Remediation orchestration layer that can propose and, when configured, apply changes (e.g., switch routing, rollback prompt/data version, disable a failing tool) with human approval.
RCA UI or CLI to surface ranked hypotheses, evidence, and suggested actions to on-call engineers.

process.triggering: Same synthetic incident replays as in the baseline, but RCA-specific alerts are enabled (e.g., hallucination-rate anomaly, cost/latency regression for a route, spike in tool errors).
process.investigation: On-call engineer primarily uses the RCA UI/CLI and ranked hypotheses. Manual dashboards are allowed only as a secondary source (usage should be noted).
process.remediation: Engineer uses the remediation orchestrator to apply or approve suggested actions when safe; otherwise they follow manual runbooks. All actions are logged as RCA decisions.
process.documentation: RCA system auto-logs hypotheses, selected root cause, evidence, and remediation steps; engineer annotates correctness and fills any missing details in the incident record.

workloads.description: Case Study I (15.2): A RAG-based LLM service experiences a sudden spike in hallucinations shortly after a data refresh job introduces corrupted or incomplete knowledge-base entries.

traffic_profile.pattern: Mixed read-heavy workload simulating user Q&A across multiple topics with a stable request rate; incident is introduced via a data-refresh replay, not load spikes.

phases.name: warmup-stable
phases.behavior: Stable request rate using a curated query set with known correct answers, low baseline hallucination rate.

phases.name: incident-introduction
phases.behavior: Trigger a data-refresh pipeline job that loads an altered index (missing or corrupted documents) and serve traffic only from the new index; hallucination rate increases sharply.

phases.name: post-incident-steady
phases.behavior: Maintain same query mix; hallucination rate remains elevated until remediation restores the correct index or adjusts retrieval configuration.

incident_script.root_cause_ground_truth: Corrupted/incorrectly filtered retrieval index produced by the latest data-refresh job, causing the retriever to return missing/irrelevant supporting documents and triggering hallucinations.
steps: At T0 + 20m, run the `data_refresh_corrupt_index` script from the repo to swap the retrieval index for a corrupted version (e.g., missing 40–60% of canonical answers and adding conflicting entries).
Ensure application routing and model versions remain unchanged to isolate the effect to data/knowledge base.
Verify via internal checks that retrieval recall has degraded (e.g., recall@k decreases by a predefined threshold).
expected_symptoms: Increase in hallucination evaluator scores (LLM or rule-based judges) on affected queries.
More guardrail or evaluator flags for factual inconsistency.
Stable latency/cost metrics (no major infra/routing change).

workloads.description: Case Study II (15.3): A multi-model routing layer is misconfigured to send a large portion of traffic to a slower, more expensive model variant, causing latency and cost regressions.

traffic_profile.pattern: Mixed traffic of short and long prompts routed across two or more models with a routing policy based on prompt characteristics.

phases.name: baseline-routing
phases.behavior: Routing policy correctly directs most standard traffic to a fast, cheap base model and complex queries to a slower, more capable model; baseline latency and cost are established.

phases.name: misconfiguration-introduction
phases.behavior: Apply a routing configuration change (e.g., via feature flag or config push) that mistakenly inverts or relaxes the routing rules, sending >70% of traffic to the slow/expensive model.

phases.name: post-change-operation
phases.behavior: Continue identical traffic profile; monitor for increased p95 latency, token usage, and per-request cost while functional quality remains approximately unchanged.

incident_script.root_cause_ground_truth: Routing configuration error that shifts most traffic to a slower, higher-cost model without a corresponding increase in quality.
steps: At T0 + 15m, deploy the `bad_routing_config` from the repo (e.g., a YAML/JSON config or feature flag change) to the routing service.
Confirm via routing logs that the percentage of traffic hitting the slow/expensive model exceeds the predefined threshold (e.g., from 20% to 80%).
Keep data, prompts, and model versions constant; only routing behavior changes.
expected_symptoms: Sharp increase in route-level p95/p99 latency and average tokens per request.
Increased cost per request and total cost over the test window.
Business KPIs (e.g., user success rate) remain mostly stable, indicating a performance/cost-only regression.
Routing decision logs show a distribution shift toward the more expensive model.

workloads.description: Case Study III (15.4): A tool-based agent workflow experiences cascading failures when a critical external tool (e.g., payments, search, or internal API) starts returning intermittent errors or malformed responses.

traffic_profile.pattern: User requests that frequently trigger tool calls (e.g., retrieval, external API lookups, or transactional operations) within an LLM-powered agent.

phases.name: healthy-tools
phases.behavior: All tools respond within expected latency and error budgets; agent successfully completes most tasks end-to-end.

phases.name: tool-degradation
phases.behavior: Inject partial failures using the repo’s `flaky_tool` script: elevated error rates (e.g., 30–50% 5xx), timeouts, or malformed payloads for a single high-dependency tool.

phases.name: tool-outage
phases.behavior: Escalate to near-total tool failure for a period (e.g., >90% failure rate, or consistently malformed responses) to simulate a hard dependency outage.

phases.name: recovery-phase
phases.behavior: Tool behavior returns to normal after remediation; observe whether the agent and application recover gracefully.

incident_script.root_cause_ground_truth: Integration failure with a single external tool (e.g., misconfigured endpoint, auth token expiry, or API contract change) causing cascading failures in the agent workflow.
steps: At T0 + 20m, run the `tool_flakiness_injector` from the repo against the selected tool endpoint (e.g., via proxy or fault-injection middleware).
At T0 + 35m, increase the severity to simulate a full outage or complete contract change.
Keep the core LLM model, prompts, and routing constant to isolate failures to the tool integration layer.
expected_symptoms: Spike in tool invocation errors (5xx, 4xx, or validation failures) and timeouts.
Increase in agent-level failures (e.g., incomplete task execution, fallback behavior, or user-visible errors).
Potential second-order effects such as elevated latency and increased token usage (retries, compensating behavior).
RCA signals linking user-facing failures to specific tool call traces and error patterns.

randomization.engineer_assignment: Use at least two engineers with similar experience levels; randomize assignment of baseline vs. treatment across incidents and participants via a Latin-square design to reduce learning and order effects.
randomization.incident_order: Randomize the order of the three incident workloads for each participant so that not all participants see incidents in the same sequence.
randomization.role_blinding: Where practical, participants should not be told whether they are in the 'baseline' or 'treatment' condition; environments should be visually similar except for RCA tooling availability.

environment_parity.identical_app_version: Use the same application, model versions, prompt templates, and infrastructure configuration for both baseline and treatment runs, differing only in the availability of RCA components.
environment_parity.identical_traffic: For each incident scenario, use deterministic replay (fixed seed and request sequence) for both baseline and treatment to ensure identical workloads.
environment_parity.time_isolation: Run baseline and treatment experiments in time-separated windows or on separate namespaces/clusters to avoid cross-run interference.

operator_guidelines.training: Provide all participants with identical, minimal orientation for both environments, focusing on capabilities rather than step-by-step guidance to avoid bias.
operator_guidelines.runbooks: Ensure the same remediation runbooks are available for both conditions; in treatment, the RCA system may suggest which runbook to follow.
operator_guidelines.documentation_template: Use a standard incident template for logging timestamps, suspected and final root causes, steps, and remediation for both baseline and treatment runs.

metrics.name: time_to_detection
metrics.definition: Elapsed time from the moment the incident condition is programmatically introduced (T_incident_start) to the moment the engineer acknowledges a concrete incident alert or manually records an incident start in the run log.

metrics.name: time_to_first_hypothesis
metrics.definition: Elapsed time from T_incident_start to the time the engineer records the first explicit root-cause hypothesis in the incident log.

metrics.name: mttr
metrics.definition: Mean time to recover: elapsed time from T_incident_start to the moment key service-level indicators return to within a predefined healthy band and the engineer confirms incident resolution.

metrics.name: hypothesis_accuracy
metrics.definition: Fraction of experiments where the final documented root cause matches the ground-truth root cause category and main contributing factor for the incident scenario.

metrics.name: false_diagnosis_rate
metrics.definition: Fraction of experiments where a primary root cause is logged that does not match the ground truth, or where remediation is applied to a non-causal component before correcting the actual root cause.

metrics.name: num_hypotheses_considered
metrics.definition: Total number of distinct root-cause hypotheses recorded by the engineer or generated and seriously evaluated by the RCA system prior to resolution.

metrics.name: investigation_effort
metrics.definition: Total active time an engineer spends on diagnosis and remediation tasks per incident, excluding waiting times when no action is taken.

metrics.name: alert_precision
metrics.definition: For detection alerts fired during incident windows, the fraction that correspond to true incidents (as opposed to noise or unaffected components).

metrics.name: alert_recall
metrics.definition: Fraction of ground-truth incidents (one per scenario run) that are correctly surfaced by at least one high-priority alert within a predefined detection window.

metrics.name: automation_uptake
metrics.definition: In the treatment condition, fraction of remediation steps executed via the remediation orchestrator (with or without human approval) versus manual direct changes.

primary.target: At least 30% reduction in median MTTR for each incident type (hallucination spike, routing regression, tool failure) in the treatment condition relative to the baseline, measured across all runs.
At least 30% reduction in median time-to-detection in the treatment condition compared to baseline for each incident type.
Absolute false-diagnosis rate in the treatment condition is not higher than in the baseline, and ideally reduced by at least 20% relative.

secondary.target: Hypothesis accuracy in the treatment condition is >= 0.8 and at least 10 percentage points higher than baseline for at least two of the three incident types.
Median investigation effort (person-minutes) is reduced by >= 20% in the treatment condition while meeting or exceeding accuracy targets.
In the treatment condition, alert precision is >= 0.7 for LLM-specific RCA alerts (hallucination, routing, tool failures).
In the treatment condition, alert recall is >= 0.9 across all incident runs.

interpretation_notes: If MTTR and time-to-detection improvements are achieved but false_diagnosis_rate increases materially, automation may be overconfident; this should be called out as a key lesson learned (15.7).
Even if quantitative targets are not met, qualitative improvements such as more structured hypotheses or clearer evidence trails should be documented to inform deployment decisions.

failure_modes.name: environment_drift_between_runs
failure_modes.description: Baseline and treatment runs are not performed on equivalent environments (e.g., different model versions, hardware, or observability setups), invalidating comparisons.
mitigations: Automate environment creation using infrastructure-as-code (e.g., Terraform, Helm charts) pinned to specific versions.
Validate equivalence by running a pre-experiment smoke test comparing key metrics (latency, error rates) between environments before injecting incidents.

failure_modes.name: operator_learning_effects
failure_modes.description: Engineers become familiar with specific incident patterns after the first run, biasing subsequent runs and favoring whichever condition is executed later.
mitigations: Randomize the order of baseline and treatment for each incident per participant.
Use multiple participants and apply a Latin-square assignment of (participant, scenario, condition, order).
Analyze results both per-run and per-participant to identify and discuss learning effects.

failure_modes.name: inconsistent_incident_injection
failure_modes.description: Incident injection scripts produce different severities or timing across baseline and treatment runs.
mitigations: Use deterministic seeds and scripted incident triggers with explicit timestamps relative to workload start.
Log all incident injection parameters and verify them post-run as part of quality checks.
Run small dry runs for each scenario to confirm consistent behavior before formal measurements.

failure_modes.name: ambiguous_ground_truth_root_cause
failure_modes.description: Incident scenarios are complex enough that multiple plausible root causes exist, making hypothesis accuracy hard to score objectively.
mitigations: Design each scenario with a single primary, clearly documented root cause and a small number of allowed contributing factors.
Encode ground truth in machine-readable form in the experiment configuration (e.g., component IDs, change IDs).
Use a rubric with categorical scoring (correct primary cause, correct contributing factor, wrong cause) for evaluating hypotheses.

failure_modes.name: alert_fatigue_and_noise
failure_modes.description: Excessive alerts or noisy detectors in the treatment condition may slow down engineers or mask useful RCA signals.
mitigations: Calibrate detectors using pre-experiment calibration runs, ensuring thresholds yield acceptable precision and recall.
Limit the number of alert types used in this experiment to those directly relevant to the incident scenarios.
Log and analyze the number of alerts per run to contextualize MTTR and detection metrics.

failure_modes.name: over-reliance_on_automation
failure_modes.description: Engineers may accept automated RCA hypotheses and remediation suggestions uncritically, leading to fast but incorrect actions.
mitigations: Train participants to treat RCA output as decision support, not ground truth, and to document when they disagree with the system.
Track when automation-led remediation targets an incorrect component and count these towards the false_diagnosis_rate.
Include scenario variants where automation suggestions are intentionally pessimistic or incomplete to encourage critical review.

failure_modes.name: metric_instrumentation_gaps
failure_modes.description: Missing or misconfigured instrumentation for hallucinations, routing, or tool calls prevents RCA components from functioning correctly.
mitigations: Run a pre-experiment instrumentation validation step that replays a small workload and verifies expected signals in the RCA data store.
Add runtime checks in the experiment harness that fail fast if key signals are missing (e.g., hallucination scores, routing logs, tool call results).

infrastructure.compute: Kubernetes cluster or equivalent container orchestration environment with at least 3–5 nodes (or VM equivalents) sufficient to run the sample LLM stack, RCA services, and load generators.
infrastructure.networking: Internal network connectivity between application, RCA services, data stores, and external/mock tools; optional internet access for external LLM APIs, or local models if air-gapped.
infrastructure.storage: Persistent storage for logs, traces, metrics, and RCA feature stores (e.g., PostgreSQL, object storage, or a columnar analytics store).

software_stack.language_runtime: Python 3.10+ for experiment harnesses and RCA components.
software_stack.orchestration: Kubernetes (minikube, kind, or cloud-managed), or docker-compose for simplified local setups.
observability: OpenTelemetry SDKs/instrumentation for the sample services.
Metrics backend such as Prometheus and a dashboarding tool (Grafana) or similar.
Log storage such as Elasticsearch, Loki, or file-based logs consumed by the RCA system.
software_stack.rca_system: Deployment of the companion repository’s RCA components: ingestion, detection/localization, hypothesis generation, remediation orchestrator, and incident replay harness.
llm_components: Access to an LLM endpoint (cloud-hosted or local) used in the examples (or a compatible model with similar APIs).
RAG components (vector store, retriever) and data-refresh scripts for Case Study I.
Routing layer with configurable model selection policies for Case Study II.
Agent framework with pluggable tools for Case Study III.

datasets_and_config.hallucination_eval_set: Curated set of Q&A pairs with ground-truth answers used to detect hallucinations and evaluate incident severity for Case Study I.
datasets_and_config.retrieval_corpus_variants: Healthy and corrupted retrieval indices for Case Study I stored in a reproducible format (e.g., two separate vector stores or index snapshots).
datasets_and_config.routing_configs: Baseline and misconfigured routing policies stored as versioned configuration files (YAML/JSON) for Case Study II.
datasets_and_config.tool_endpoints: Mock or real external tool endpoints with controlled behavior; fault-injection scripts or proxies to produce flaky and outage conditions for Case Study III.
datasets_and_config.experiment_config_files: YAML/JSON definitions for each scenario, including workload parameters, incident timings, and ground-truth annotations.

prerequisites: Ensure Python 3.10+ and Docker (and optionally Kubernetes/minikube) are installed.
Set environment variables or config files for LLM API access (or start local models as described in the repo).
Install required Python dependencies via `pip install -r requirements.txt` or the equivalent per the repo instructions.
setup_steps: Navigate to the `experiments/ch15_e2e_case_studies/` directory in the repository.
Deploy the base LLM application stack using the provided scripts (e.g., `make deploy-app` or `kubectl apply -f k8s/app/`).
Deploy observability components (metrics, logs, traces) and confirm basic telemetry is flowing (e.g., via Grafana dashboards or CLI tools).
Deploy the RCA stack (ingestion, detection, hypothesis generation, remediation) using the provided manifests (e.g., `make deploy-rca` or `kubectl apply -f k8s/rca/`).
Run the instrumentation validation script (e.g., `python validate_instrumentation.py`) to ensure hallucination scores, routing logs, and tool traces are correctly captured.
Prepare or verify the scenario assets: healthy/corrupted retrieval indices, routing configs, and tool fault-injection scripts according to the README in `experiments/ch15_e2e_case_studies/assets/`.
execution_steps: For each incident scenario (hallucination spike, routing regression, tool failure), and for each condition (baseline, treatment):
1. Select participant and assign condition and scenario order according to your Latin-square or randomization plan.
2. Start the appropriate environment:
- Baseline: Deploy the application stack without RCA services, or run the stack with RCA components disabled via config flags.
- Treatment: Deploy the full stack including all RCA components and ensure alerts and remediation orchestrator are enabled.
3. Start the workload generator using the scenario-specific script, for example:
- `python run_workload.py --scenario cs1_hallucination_spike --config configs/cs1_baseline.yaml`
- Use the same workload configuration for both baseline and treatment (only the `--env` or similar flag differs).
4. At the configured incident injection time (or automatically via the harness), trigger the incident script:
- Case Study I: `python inject_incident.py --scenario cs1_hallucination_spike --mode corrupt_index`
- Case Study II: `python inject_incident.py --scenario cs2_routing_regression --mode bad_routing_config`
- Case Study III: `python inject_incident.py --scenario cs3_tool_failure --mode flaky_then_outage`
5. Instruct the participant to respond as if on-call, following the condition-specific investigation process:
- Baseline: Use only standard dashboards/logs plus runbooks.
- Treatment: Use the RCA UI/CLI, alerts, and remediation orchestrator as the primary tools, with dashboards as secondary.
6. Throughout the incident, the participant should:
- Record timestamps when they notice an issue, when they formulate each hypothesis, and when they apply remediation.
- Mark which hypotheses they consider and which they accept as the final root cause.
- Record each remediation action (including automated ones) and its effect.
7. Let the workload run until recovery is confirmed and at least several minutes of post-recovery data are collected for metric computation.
8. Stop the workload and export experiment logs via the provided script, for example:
- `python export_evidence.py --scenario cs1_hallucination_spike --run_id <RUN_ID>`
9. Repeat for all assigned scenarios and conditions, ensuring randomization and environment reset between runs.
post_run_steps: Run the analysis script (e.g., `python analyze_runs.py --config analysis/ch15_config.yaml`) to compute metrics such as time_to_detection, mttr, hypothesis_accuracy, and false_diagnosis_rate for each run.
Inspect the generated reports (CSV/JSON summaries, plots) for each scenario and condition; store them under `experiments/ch15_e2e_case_studies/results/`.
Review qualitative logs (hypotheses history, RCA suggestions, engineer notes) to extract lessons learned and observed anti-patterns, feeding into section 15.7.
Optionally, iterate on RCA configurations (e.g., alert thresholds, hypothesis prompts) and re-run experiments to observe how tuning affects outcomes.

run_metadata.run_id: string (unique identifier for an individual experiment run)
run_metadata.timestamp_incident_injected: ISO 8601 datetime at which the incident script executed
run_metadata.timestamp_detection: ISO 8601 datetime when engineer or system first recognized the incident
run_metadata.timestamp_first_hypothesis: ISO 8601 datetime when the first root-cause hypothesis was recorded
run_metadata.timestamp_recovery_confirmed: ISO 8601 datetime when the system was considered recovered
run_metadata.participant_id: string (pseudonymous identifier for the on-call engineer)
run_metadata.environment_version: string (git commit hash, container image tag, or configuration version)
run_metadata.notes: string (free-text notes about anomalies or deviations from protocol)

incident_ground_truth.root_cause_contributing: array of strings (optional secondary factors, e.g., 'missing_alert', 'insufficient_retry_policy')

hypotheses.timestamp: ISO 8601 datetime when the hypothesis was first proposed
hypotheses.description: string (natural language description of suspected root cause)
hypotheses.confidence_score: number (0.0–1.0) if generated by RCA system, null if N/A

selected_root_cause.timestamp_selected: ISO 8601 datetime when hypothesis was accepted as primary root cause

alerts.is_true_positive: boolean (does this alert correspond to the injected incident?)
alerts.acknowledged_timestamp: ISO 8601 datetime when the engineer acknowledged the alert, if applicable

detection_summary.primary_detection_alert_id: string (ID of the alert most directly associated with detection, if any)
detection_summary.detection_notes: string (free-text context about how incident was first noticed)

remediation_actions.target_component: string (identifier of affected service, tool, or configuration)
remediation_actions.notes: string (free-text, including links to logs or dashboards if relevant)

time_series_metrics.sampling_interval_seconds: number (interval at which metrics are sampled for storage in the experiment logs)

service_metrics.hallucination_rate: number (proportion of evaluated requests flagged as hallucinations, for applicable scenarios)
service_metrics.tool_error_rate: number (proportion of tool invocations failing, for applicable scenarios)

rca_internal_signals.retrieval_recall_estimate: number (e.g., recall@k or proxy score; Case Study I)
rca_internal_signals.routing_distribution: object mapping model_id:string -> traffic_fraction:number (Case Study II)
rca_internal_signals.tool_health_scores: object mapping tool_id:string -> health_score:number (Case Study III)
